notes.back: Flight with no sideslip: the airplane presents its smallest profile to the relative wind, so drag is at its minimum.
notes.explanation: With both engines running this is simply coordinated flight with the ball centred; with one engine out it needs a particular aileron and rudder combination.
notes.example: Like a yaw string taped to the windshield pointing straight up the middle: the relative wind meets the nose head-on.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Inoperative Flight Principles"
notes.evidence: This is a condition of zero sideslip, and the airplane is presenting its smallest possible profile to the relative wind. As a result, drag is at its minimum.

notes.front: With one engine inoperative, does a centred ball show zero sideslip?
notes.back: No: asymmetric thrust means the centred ball is no longer the indicator, and no flight deck instrument shows it directly.
notes.explanation: Without a yaw string, the pilot sets a predetermined bank angle and ball position instead.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Inoperative Flight Principles"
notes.evidence: In a multiengine airplane with an inoperative engine, the centered ball is no longer the indicator of zero sideslip due to asymmetric thrust. In fact, there is no flight deck instrument that directly indicates conditions for zero sideslip.

notes.front: Without specific guidance, what bank and ball position give zero sideslip with one engine inoperative?
notes.back: About 2° of bank toward the operating engine, with the ball one-third to one-half deflected toward it.
notes.explanation: The one-engine-inoperative performance charts were determined at zero sideslip, so this attitude is needed to get the charted climb.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Failure After Lift-off", "Climb"
notes.evidence: Without specific guidance for zero sideslip, a bank of 2° and one-third to one-half ball deflection on the slip/skid indicator toward the operative engine is suggested.

notes.front: After the left engine fails and is feathered, you climb straight ahead at best single-engine rate of climb speed. Which way, and about how much, do you bank?
notes.back: About 2° to the right, toward the operating engine ("raise the dead").
notes.explanation: Wings level with the ball centred needs large rudder and leaves a moderate sideslip, which reduces climb performance.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Failure After Lift-off"
notes.evidence: The phrase “raise the dead” is a reminder that the best climb performance is obtained with a very shallow bank, about 2° toward the operating engine.
uses: best single-engine rate of climb speed

notes.front: If an engine fails on the takeoff roll below the minimum control speed, what should the pilot do?
notes.back: Reject the takeoff: promptly close both throttles and keep directional control with rudder and brakes.
notes.explanation: Airborne below that speed, directional control is not possible with the other engine at takeoff power.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Takeoff and Climb"
notes.evidence: If an engine fails below VMC while the airplane is on the ground, the takeoff needs to be rejected. Directional control can only be maintained by promptly closing both throttles and using rudder and brakes as required.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: An engine fails shortly after lift-off. What decides whether to continue the climb or land?
notes.back: Whether single-engine climb performance is adequate, with the airplane promptly and correctly configured.
notes.explanation: If a climb is unlikely or impossible, the landing is made in the most suitable area, even off-airport.

image.alt: A decision diagram. One engine fails shortly after lift-off. Question: is single-engine climb performance adequate, with the airplane promptly and correctly configured? Yes leads to: the climb may be continued. No, climb unlikely, leads to: land in the most suitable area, even off-airport. A note warns that continuing flight beyond the airplane's performance capability is to be avoided above all.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13, "Engine Failure After Lift-off" (see Figure 13-6)

notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Failure After Lift-off"
notes.evidence: If single-engine climb performance is adequate for continued flight, and the airplane has been promptly and correctly configured, the climb after takeoff may be continued.

notes.front: Is the red radial minimum control speed on the airspeed indicator a fixed speed in all conditions?
notes.back: No: it holds only for the conditions used in certification; in practice it can be lower or higher.
notes.explanation: The speed varies with conditions and pilot technique.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Derivation of VMC"
notes.evidence: VMC is a fixed airspeed only for the very specific set of circumstances under which it was determined during aircraft certification.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative

notes.front: On an engine-inoperative approach, if the gear is lowered on downwind, by when should it be confirmed down?
notes.back: No later than abeam the intended point of landing.
notes.explanation: The pattern is flown at similar altitudes, speeds and key positions as a two-engine approach, with more power on the operating engine.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "Engine Inoperative Approach and Landing"
notes.evidence: With adequate airspeed and performance, the landing gear can still be extended on the downwind leg. In which case it should be confirmed DOWN no later than abeam the intended point of landing.

notes.front: Why must a minimum control speed demonstration never be allowed to become a single-engine stall?
notes.back: A stall with high asymmetrical thrust may cause an unrecoverable loss of control and a fatal accident.
notes.explanation: Any sign of an impending stall means ending the demonstration at once.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 13 "Transition to Multiengine Airplanes", "VMC Demonstration"
notes.evidence: A VMC demonstration that is allowed to degrade into a single-engine stall with high asymmetrical thrust may result in an unrecoverable loss of control and a fatal accident.
uses: minimum control speed with the critical engine inoperative
